label: Chapter 5: Napoleon, Waterloo and the Revolution of 1830

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The French years were short. But they changed Brussels more than almost any other period, didn't they?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did. After the annexation of 1795, the revolutionary government sets about erasing the old order.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Monasteries and convents are closed, and their lands and buildings sold off.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many medieval churches and abbeys, some of them centuries old, are demolished or turned into barracks, warehouses, and factories.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ouch. And the guilds? The ones that rebuilt the Grand Place?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Abolished. Feudal privileges disappear.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In their place, France introduces new laws, new weights and measures, and eventually the Napoleonic Code, which becomes the basis of Belgian civil law.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did ordinary people think?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most unpopular novelty was conscription.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Young men from Brussels and its countryside were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came back.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Did Napoleon himself ever come to Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than once. He used the royal estate at Laeken, on the northern edge of the city, as a residence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It would later become the home of the Belgian royal family.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And even after his fall, the artist who had painted his coronation, Jacques-Louis David, chose Brussels as his place of exile.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He lived there from 1816 until he died in 1825.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the emperor's painter retires to Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a good place to be an exile.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the end of the empire came uncomfortably close.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How close?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very close. In 1814, Napoleon is defeated and exiled, and the Congress of Vienna, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, redraws the map.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great powers decide France's northern neighbors need to be stronger.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So they combine the old Austrian Netherlands with the Dutch Republic to create a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, under King William the First.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: With two capitals, I seem to remember.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Government and parliament met alternately in The Hague and in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That sounds exhausting. Imagine the moving vans.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every session, off they go.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then Napoleon comes back.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In March of 1815, he escapes from the island of Elba and returns to France.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For about a hundred days, he rules again, and he marches north to strike the allied armies gathering in Belgium, under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Field Marshal Blücher.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels in June of 1815 is full of British officers and their families.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Allied officers and their families, yes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the evening of the fifteenth of June, the Duchess of Richmond holds a famous ball in the city for Wellington and his officers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the middle of the evening, news arrives that Napoleon's army has crossed the border and is advancing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And they just left?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Officers slip out of the ball, still in their dress uniforms, and march south to fight.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The scene becomes so famous that the poet Lord Byron, who visits Brussels a year later, writes some of his best-known verses about that night of dancing and the sound of guns.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's one way to leave a party.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the most famous early exit in history.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And three days later, Waterloo.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the eighteenth of June, the decisive battle is fought at a village about fifteen kilometers south of Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On that field, the Allied armies, with Wellington's British, Dutch, and Belgian troops and Blücher's Prussians, crush Napoleon's army and end his career for good.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And in Brussels, they could hear it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People could hear the cannon. And in the days that followed, the city was filled with thousands of wounded soldiers, treated in houses, churches, and makeshift hospitals.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So then the new kingdom gets to work.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King William is a hardworking, practical ruler who promotes industry, canals, schools, and a modern economy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels flourishes. The city gets a new opera house, the Théâtre de la Monnaie, which opens in 1819, on the site of the old royal mint.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the kingdom had a flaw built in.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Didn't it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A basic one. The north is mostly Protestant and Dutch-speaking.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The south is mostly Catholic, with a French-speaking upper class and a Dutch-speaking Flemish population.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the king favors the Dutch language and the north in appointments and taxation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So who's angry?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: French-speaking liberals resent his controls over the press and the schools.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Catholics resent his interference in the church.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1828, these two groups, who normally dislike each other, join forces against the king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the beginning of the end.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. A king so unpopular that liberals and Catholics team up.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's an achievement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A very unusual one.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then, the night at the opera.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-fifth of August, 1830, there's a performance at the Monnaie of a popular French opera called The Mute Girl of Portici.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It tells the story of a revolt in seventeenth-century Naples against Spanish rule, and it contains a stirring duet about love of country.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the audience got carried away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As the singers reach that number, the audience is swept up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They pour out of the theater into the streets, shouting, and join crowds that are already angry about food prices and unemployment.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the next days, mobs attack the houses of unpopular officials and the offices of a pro-government newspaper.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Similar riots break out in other towns.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So a revolution started because of a song.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A song, and food prices, and a lot of resentment.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But, yes. The song lit the match.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Was it meant to be a revolution?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At first it was a protest, and its leaders wanted autonomy, not independence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But King William hesitates, then sends troops under his son, Prince Frederick, to restore order.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-third of September, some ten thousand Dutch soldiers enter Brussels through the gates on the upper side of the city and try to push down the hill toward the old center.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And who stopped them?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A ragged force of volunteers. Workers, students, craftsmen, and men from other towns, including Liège, who had come to help.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For four days, from the twenty-third to the twenty-sixth of September, the fighting rages around the Royal Park, in the streets, from house to house, over barricades made of paving stones, carts, and furniture.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the end of the fourth night, the Dutch have pulled back.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Stubbornness tally?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Volunteers with paving stones beating a trained army?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's five. At least.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Five. I'm writing it down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A provisional government has already taken control in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And on the fourth of October, it declares Belgium independent.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A National Congress is elected, and in February of 1831 it adopts a constitution that's among the most liberal in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Guarantees of freedom of the press, of religion, and of association, and a king with limited powers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who did they pick as king?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Congress chooses Brussels as the capital, and it needs a king acceptable to the great powers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After much negotiation, they pick a German prince, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, a widower of the British royal family and an uncle to the future Queen Victoria.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Imported king. Okay.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the date everyone in Belgium knows.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-first of July, 1831, Leopold stands on the steps of a church on the Place Royale and swears an oath to the constitution.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That day, July twenty-first, is still Belgium's National Day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the Dutch weren't ready to accept it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. A few weeks later, in August of 1831, the Dutch army invades, in what's called the Ten Days' Campaign.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A French army has to march in to save Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It takes years of negotiation before the Dutch accept the loss.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it was settled in 1839.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By a treaty signed in London that finally confirms Belgium's independence, and guarantees the new country's perpetual neutrality, under the protection of the great powers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The same treaty, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, splits the old duchy of Luxembourg in two, and hands its western half, including the town of Bastogne, to Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Two places to visit for this chapter?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the Place des Martyrs, a quiet neoclassical square near the city center, a monument and a crypt honor the fighters who died in the September days of 1830.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the Parc de Bruxelles, the same park where the Dutch troops fought their way in and lost, you can walk among the trees and statues where the battle for Belgian independence was won.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next, the capital of a new kingdom grows into a modern metropolis.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the king who rules it from 1865 turns it into a showcase.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Financed, in part, by a colony of terrible cruelty.
